props.title: Deep Learning
props.sub: networks that learn their own filters

captions: Part three.
Deep learning.
This is the turning point.

Here the machine stops using the filters
we
hand it,

and starts inventing its own — learned
from
data,
not designed by us.

This single shift is what changed computer
vision
forever.
Let's understand exactly why it works.
You might reasonably ask — why invent a
special kind of network for images?
Why not just take that grid of pixels,
flatten it into one long list,

and feed it into an ordinary neural
network?
Connect every pixel to every neuron,
and let it figure everything out.
There are two problems,
and they are both serious.
The first problem is size.

A modest image has hundreds of thousands
of
pixels.
If you connect every one of them to
every neuron in the next layer,

you get billions of connections in a
single
layer.
That is far too many numbers to store
or train.
It would be hopeless.

The second problem is that this approach
throws
away two obvious truths about images.
Truth number one — meaning is local.
To find an eye,
you only need to look at a small
patch of the picture.
You do not need the opposite corner.
Truth number two — a pattern means the
same thing wherever it appears.

An edge in the top-left corner looks
exactly
like an edge in the bottom-right corner.
So why on earth would we learn to
detect it twice,
in two separate places?

The convolutional neural network is
designed to respect
both truths.
It uses small filters that only look at
little local patches.
That handles locality.
And it slides the very same filter across
the entire image,
reusing it everywhere.
That handles repetition.
The payoff is huge.
Far fewer numbers to learn,

and every detector automatically works no
matter where
the pattern shows up.
That is the trick that finally made vision
learnable at scale.
